# Anchors, Halos, and Decoys {#when-context-rewrites-comparison}

*When Context Rewrites Comparison*

::: {#chapter-11-start .chapter-epigraph}
> “Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.”
>
> — Oscar Wilde, [*The Picture of Dorian Gray*](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/174/pg174-images.html), 1891, ch. IV
:::

You are choosing between online access and a more expensive print-plus-online subscription. Then a third offer appears: print alone at exactly the same price as print plus online. You would never buy it, yet the combined offer suddenly looks easier to justify.

The added option has changed no feature of the original two. It has made an easy comparison available, even though the real question remains whether you would use enough of the extra service to justify its cost. Similar shifts can occur when a first number starts a discussion or one favorable impression colors everything that follows. To make the judgment answer to your objective, you need to identify which comparison is doing the work.

::: {.callout-note .core-idea icon=false}
## Core Idea

A starting number, an overall impression, or the surrounding menu can influence judgment. These are different effects and require different checks: prepare an independent estimate, examine each criterion, or test the choice without the extra option.

:::

## Learning goals

- Explain anchoring and insufficient adjustment.
- Separate a global halo or horn impression from dimension-specific evidence.
- Test whether a preference survives removal or rearrangement of a decoy.
- Explain how evaluating options together, separately, or through a different response task can change their apparent value.


## Anchoring: how a starting number shapes an estimate {#the-first-number-enters-first}

An uncertain estimate needs a starting point. The first available number supplies one, but it can also pull the judgment toward a value with little connection to the question. For a budget or an offer, that starting point can shape how much is spent or conceded.

**Anchoring** occurs when an initial value influences later judgment, even if the value is arbitrary or irrelevant. In Tversky and Kahneman's (1974) demonstration, a wheel supplied a number before participants estimated the percentage of United Nations members that were African countries. They first judged whether the percentage was above or below the number, then gave an estimate. Groups starting from **10** produced a median estimate of **25%**; groups starting from **65** produced a median of **45%**. The wheel supplied no evidence about UN membership, yet the estimates remained twenty percentage points apart.

One possible route is insufficient adjustment: the estimate moves away from the starting point, but not far enough. Another is selective accessibility, in which considering an anchor makes compatible information easier to retrieve (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997). [Chapter 13](13-accessibility-familiarity-and-ease.qmd#accessibility-memory-prepares-an-answer) develops that memory mechanism.

In a budget discussion, last year's figure may become the starting point before anyone examines current needs. A negotiation offer can similarly establish a range that later discussion struggles to leave. Whether that influence is useful depends on the number's relevance and evidence.

Ariely, Loewenstein, and Prelec (2003) showed that even arbitrary anchors, such as the last two digits of a social security number, could influence willingness to pay for consumer goods. Participants first considered whether they would pay an amount equal to those digits, then stated their maximum willingness to pay. Higher arbitrary numbers led to higher valuations. The result illustrates how fragile valuation can be when people lack stable reference points.

Anchoring is not always irrational. In many situations, first estimates contain useful information. If an expert provides a starting estimate, it may be reasonable to use it. The problem is that anchors influence judgment even when they are irrelevant, extreme, strategic, or weakly justified.

A practical defense is to collect estimates and their evidence before the proposed number is revealed. Once an anchor is known, imagining that it was never seen is an imperfect substitute. Independent market data or a fresh estimate from someone who has not seen the proposal may add more than another adjustment to the original number.

![Two distinct empirical patterns. Anchoring means that an available number can shift a later estimate toward it; insufficient adjustment and selective accessibility are among several proposed mechanisms. The attraction effect means that adding an asymmetrically dominated decoy can increase the choice share of the option that dominates it.](../figures/anchor-decoy.svg){#fig-anchor-decoy fig-alt="The anchoring panel separates the observed shift toward an available number from four possible mechanisms: insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility, scale use, and conversational inference. The attraction-effect panel shows options A and B, then an inferior decoy B-minus, and states that adding the decoy can increase B's choice share."}

@fig-anchor-decoy deliberately separates **effect** from **mechanism**. “Insufficient adjustment” is not a complete definition of anchoring: anchor-consistent information can become selectively accessible, and scale use or conversational inferences can also contribute in some tasks (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997). Asymmetric dominance defines the decoy relation (Huber et al., 1982). The diagnostic question is therefore first whether the context changed judgment, and then which mechanism the evidence can distinguish.

## Halo and horn effects

An engaging interview gives the committee evidence about how the candidate comes across. It can nevertheless make reliability or technical ability seem established before either has been tested. A decision that needs several kinds of evidence may then rest on a single impression.

The halo effect occurs when an overall impression influences judgments of specific traits. A positive impression in one area spills over into unrelated judgments. A negative impression can produce a “horn effect,” where one negative quality colors everything else (Thorndike, 1920).

The traits need not be unrelated in reality. The concern is whether the assessment rests on evidence about their relationship or simply extends one favorable impression. The committee needs to know which ratings have independent support.

Solomon Asch’s classic work on impression formation showed that the order and valence of traits shape overall impressions. A person described as intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, and envious is judged differently from a person described with the same traits in reverse order (Asch, 1946). Early information shapes the frame through which later information is interpreted.

Nisbett and Wilson (1977a) demonstrated a halo effect in evaluations of a lecturer. Participants watched the same instructor behave either warmly or coldly. Those who saw the warm version rated not only his personality but also his appearance, mannerisms, and accent more favorably. They often did not realize that their global impression had influenced specific judgments.

Business analysis can suffer from the same problem when successful results prompt favorable retrospective ratings of leadership, culture, and strategy (Rosenzweig, 2007). Outcome knowledge changes the overall impression, then the impression seems to explain the outcome.

For a hiring decision, gather comparable evidence for each criterion before forming the overall assessment. Rate technical work from a work sample, for example, and record the evidence for reliability separately. An early awkward answer or a confident manner should not silently determine every rating.

## The decoy changes the comparison

Rejecting an inferior offer should leave us free to assess the remaining options on their merits. Yet the act of comparing them with that offer may already have changed which one looks worthwhile. The subscription case lets us test this by holding the original options fixed and changing the surrounding menu.

The **attraction effect** occurs when adding an **asymmetrically dominated decoy** increases choice of the option that dominates it (Huber et al., 1982). The target is at least as good as the decoy on the relevant attributes and better on at least one, while the decoy is not dominated in the same way by the competing option. Suppose a customer is choosing between a cheaper online subscription and a more expensive print-plus-online subscription. If a print-only subscription is added at the same price as print-plus-online, it is clearly inferior. Rationally, it should not be chosen. Yet its presence can make the print-plus-online option look like a better deal and increase its choice share.

The proposed mechanism is relative evaluation. A customer uncertain about the usefulness of print can easily see that print plus online offers more than print alone at the same price. That comparison may receive weight before the customer has decided whether either package is worth more than online access.

Ariely (2008) reported a classroom demonstration using a subscription menu displayed on *Economist.com*. One group of 100 participants saw three options: web only for US$59, print only for US$125, and print plus web for US$125. Sixteen chose web only, nobody chose print only, and 84 chose print plus web. A different group of 100 saw the same menu without the print-only option. This time, 68 chose web only and 32 chose print plus web. The option nobody selected therefore changed the distribution of choices between the two remaining options.

![A reported classroom demonstration of the subscription decoy effect. With a dominated print-only option in the menu, 16 of 100 participants chose web only, none chose print only, and 84 chose print plus web. In a different group shown only the two target options, 68 chose web only and 32 chose print plus web. Classroom choice counts reported by Ariely (2008).](../figures/economist-subscription-decoy.svg){#fig-subscription-decoy fig-alt="Two side-by-side subscription menus show reported choices in classroom groups of 100. With a print-only decoy priced at 125 dollars, 16 chose web only at 59 dollars, none chose print only at 125 dollars, and 84 chose print plus web at 125 dollars. Without the decoy, 68 chose web only and 32 chose print plus web."}

@fig-subscription-decoy is memorable because the decoy received no choices, yet its removal changed what people selected. Huber et al. (1982) provide the experimental foundation for this attraction effect.

The easy comparison is also a boundary condition: an attraction effect need not survive when the advantage is harder to interpret. Frederick, Lee, and Baskin (2014) often failed to obtain attraction effects when people tasted products or saw attributes in pictures rather than comparing numerical ratings. Yang and Lynn (2014) likewise found much weaker effects with meaningful verbal or pictorial descriptions. Test the intended choice and presentation.

Not every menu effect is an attraction effect. An extremely expensive wine may make another price seem moderate, and an added premium package may make a middle option look like a compromise. Those examples need not contain an asymmetrically dominated decoy. Identify the actual comparison before assigning a mechanism.

For the subscription, remove print-only and evaluate what the combined package adds over online access for you. The comparison becomes harder, but it addresses the value of what you would actually use.

## Together or separately: what becomes easy to evaluate? {#evaluation-modes}

Imagine inspecting two used music dictionaries. One looks new and contains 10,000 entries; the other has a torn cover and 20,000 entries. Alone, a torn cover is easy to judge, while the adequacy of 20,000 entries may be obscure. Side by side, the difference in coverage becomes conspicuous.

Hsee (1996) used this comparison with 116 college students. Mean willingness to pay favored the larger dictionary in **joint evaluation**, but the intact dictionary in **separate evaluation**. The difference between evaluation modes was statistically significant, although the separate-evaluation contrast alone was not conventionally significant. These were hypothetical valuations, not completed purchases.

The **evaluability hypothesis** explains why an attribute can gain weight when a comparison makes its magnitude interpretable. Cover damage is readily understood without a comparison; judging the adequacy of the number of entries requires more knowledge. **A feature's weight depends partly on how well we can assess it.**

Hsee also changed evaluability directly. In a CD-changer experiment, providing a best-to-worst range for an unfamiliar sound-quality measure removed the reversal between joint and separate evaluation. The products were unchanged; the benchmark made an attribute easier to assess on its own. This supports the explanation that the comparison changes how interpretable the information is.

For the hiring committee, compare work samples on common criteria, then judge the preferred applicant against the actual job requirements. A clear ranking shows who performs better on a measure; the committee still needs to establish how much that difference matters for the work. [Chapter 6](06-valuation-how-options-become-worth-choosing.qmd#evaluability-and-attention) connects this distinction to valuation. The [focusing illusion in Chapter 22](22-deciding-for-a-better-life-satisfaction-connection-and-meaning.qmd#focusing-illusion) explains how attention to one clear advantage can displace the rest of a consequential comparison.

[]{#preference-reversal-and-prominence}

An ordering can also change when people switch response tasks. **Preference reversal** describes this inconsistency when substantively equivalent options are ranked differently under different elicitation procedures. The dictionary example changes evaluation mode; asking someone to choose between options and then price them changes what the response requires.

Tversky, Sattath, and Slovic (1988) studied another distinction: choice versus **matching**, in which a person adjusts one attribute until two options are equally attractive. Their **prominence hypothesis** proposes that the more important attribute can receive greater weight in choice than in matching. A decision-maker might accept a cost–safety trade-off while matching two programs, yet favor the safer program when later asked to choose between those matched alternatives.

The diagnostic is to compare the answers before deciding which to trust. Keep information and consequences constant, make the trade-off explicit, and ask what each response task made salient. [Chapter 17](17-prospect-theory-gains-and-losses-begin-at-a-reference-point.qmd#framing-changes-the-reference-point-but-equivalence-must-be-checked) applies the same equivalence check to gains, losses, and risk.

## Match the correction to the comparison {#three-forms-of-contextual-comparison}

An anchor influences an estimate, a halo spreads an impression across attributes, and a decoy changes the menu used to compare options. Evaluation mode and response task can change which attributes receive weight. Their shared lesson is to inspect what the setting made easy to compare; the appropriate correction depends on the pathway.

[]{#the-hiring-case-context-before-evidence}

Return to the hiring committee from [Chapter 1](01-how-decisions-should-be-made-and-how-they-actually-are.qmd#one-decision-two-questions). It wants evidence of future performance, but must first decide what counts as a plausible candidate and a useful comparison. Context can settle those questions before the evidence is examined.

One committee member proposes that a strong candidate should have “about eight years” of experience. That number can anchor later discussion even if job analysis does not justify it. The first applicant is warm, confident, and from a prestigious firm; the global impression can spill into ratings of judgment, learning, and reliability. The shortlist then includes a clearly weaker candidate whose profile resembles the prestigious applicant, making that applicant look dominant relative to the remaining candidate.

In this hypothetical case, the proposed experience requirement narrows the comparison, the favorable impression fills gaps in the evidence, and the weaker profile makes one candidate look especially strong. Trace each judgment to its source.

A structured process interrupts each pathway upstream. Define job outcomes and acceptable experience ranges before applications are discussed. Collect comparable work samples. Score evidence for each criterion independently before forming an overall judgment. Where a profile appears dominated on the agreed criteria, verify that judgment and ask whether removing it changes the comparison. Then compare the preferred candidate with an external performance standard, not merely with the designed shortlist.

[]{#redesigning-the-process}

The hiring case shows why the correction must match the comparison. More careful adjustment cannot create an estimate independent of the anchor; more discussion of the candidate cannot supply a missing work sample. @tbl-14-1 matches the diagnosed problem to a practical change informed by research on debiasing (Larrick, 2004).

| Observed effect | Context to examine | Process response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anchoring | An estimate shifts toward an initial number or range | Generate an independent estimate before seeing the anchor |
| Halo or horn effect | A global impression spills into ratings of particular attributes | Score criteria separately before discussion |
| Attraction effect | Adding an asymmetrically dominated decoy increases preference for the target | Check the choice without the decoy and compare each option with an external standard |
| Preference reversal | An ordering changes between joint and separate evaluation, or between choice, pricing, and matching | Compare responses under equivalent information; check the trade-off against the decision’s objective |
: Observed comparison effects and checks on the decision process {#tbl-14-1}

## Practice Lab

Choose one hiring, budgeting, pricing, or purchasing decision. Produce a **comparison audit** with three versions: an estimate collected before the proposed anchor is revealed, using a new case or an unexposed observer if you already know it; criterion-by-criterion ratings made before an overall impression; and the same choice menu with every dominated option removed. Report which judgments changed, which remained stable, and what external standard should govern the final comparison.

## Take it forward

The print-only offer was easy to reject. The harder question is whether the combined subscription is worth its extra cost when evaluated against what you need. Whenever an option suddenly looks compelling, identify the comparison that made it so and test whether another relevant comparison supports it.
